subject: biology-hl
about: Original practice questions written for NevaIB from the IB guide's syllabus understandings and the school's unit order. Not IB past-paper questions, not publisher material and not IB markschemes: the marking points are written for self-marking. Organisms, experiments and data in data-response items are invented for practice.

choices: The role a species plays in its community
All the populations in an area
The place where a species normally lives
The range of temperatures a species tolerates
items.note: Habitat = location (and its conditions). The role is the niche.

choices: Soil pH
Predation
Competition
Parasitism
items.note: Abiotic = non-living (temperature, light, pH, water, salinity). The others are biotic interactions.

items.stem: Marram grass has rolled leaves with stomata inside the roll. This is an adaptation to:
choices: Absorb more light on shaded forest floors
Increase gas exchange in waterlogged soil
Trap insects for extra nitrogen
Reduce water loss in dry, windy sand dunes
items.note: Rolling traps humid air around the stomata, reducing the water vapour gradient and transpiration.

items.stem: A species' range of tolerance for a factor is:
choices: The best value of the factor for growth
The limits between which it can survive
The area of land a species occupies
The number of offspring it produces
items.note: Within the range it can survive; the optimum is where it does best. Outside the limits it cannot persist.

items.stem: To study how plant distribution changes from a footpath into a meadow, the best sampling method is:
choices: A transect with quadrats placed at regular intervals
Random quadrats placed across the whole meadow and footpath
Capture–mark–release–recapture
Counting every plant in the meadow
items.note: Transects show change along an environmental gradient; random sampling estimates overall abundance.

items.stem: Coral reefs need water that is:
choices: Cold, deep, dark and rich in nutrients
Fresh, fast-flowing, muddy and nutrient-rich
Warm, deep and with no light at all
Warm, clear, shallow and low in nutrients
items.note: Reef corals rely on photosynthetic zooxanthellae, so they need light (clear, shallow water) and warmth.

items.stem: Which adaptation helps cacti survive in hot deserts?
choices: Large thin leaves to absorb more light
Shallow roots that only reach wet soil
Spines instead of leaves to reduce surface area
Many stomata open during the hottest hours
items.note: Reduced leaf area, thick stems storing water, CAM photosynthesis with stomata open at night all reduce water loss.

choices: Average daily light hours at different latitudes and altitudes
Mean monthly temperature and precipitation for a location
The number of species found in each biome
The change in population size over a year
items.note: Climographs combine temperature (line) and rainfall (bars), which largely determine the biome.

items.stem: Hot deserts and tropical rainforests differ mainly in:
choices: Temperature, which is much lower in deserts all year
Light intensity, which is low in deserts for most of the year
Precipitation, which is very low in deserts and high in rainforests
Soil pH, which is the main factor deciding the biome
items.note: Both can be warm; the large difference in rainfall determines which biome forms.

items.stem: Plants in tropical rainforests often have leaves with drip tips. This adaptation:
choices: Collects and stores water so the plant can survive the dry seasons
Lets rainwater run off quickly, reducing the growth of fungi and algae
Reduces light absorption in the bright canopy
Reduces the loss of carbon dioxide from the leaf
items.note: High rainfall and humidity encourage microbial growth on wet leaves; drip tips help them dry.

items.stem: Which observation best supports the idea that temperature limits the distribution of a plant species?
choices: It is found only below a certain altitude on all mountains studied
It grows faster when fertiliser is added
It is eaten by more herbivores in summer than in the winter months
It is found in both sunny and shaded places
items.note: A consistent upper limit linked to colder conditions at altitude suggests temperature (or a correlated factor) is limiting.

items.stem: Outline how a transect can be used to investigate the effect of an abiotic factor on plant distribution.
markscheme: Lay a tape along the environmental gradient (1)
Place quadrats at regular intervals and record species abundance/percentage cover (1)
Measure the abiotic factor (e.g. light, soil moisture) at each quadrat (1)
Repeat transects and look for correlation (1)
items.tactic: Method: sampling, measurement of the factor, analysis.

items.stem: Explain two adaptations of an animal to a hot desert.
markscheme: Example: concentrated urine / long loops of Henle reduce water loss (1)
Example: nocturnal behaviour / burrowing avoids heat (1)
Example: large ears increase heat loss (1)
Each adaptation linked to survival in heat or drought (1)
items.tactic: Each adaptation needs a "so that" consequence.

items.stem: Explain why the same biome can be found on different continents.
markscheme: Biome determined mainly by climate (temperature and rainfall) (1)
Similar climates occur at similar latitudes on different continents (1)
Similar selection pressures produce similar adaptations (convergent evolution) (1)

items.stem:
(Invented data for practice.) Percentage cover of an invented moss and light intensity were recorded along a 10 m transect from a forest edge: 0 m 2%, 1200 lux; 2 m 8%, 800 lux; 4 m 25%, 400 lux; 6 m 40%, 200 lux; 8 m 45%, 150 lux; 10 m 44%, 140 lux.
(a) Describe the relationship between light and moss cover. (b) Suggest a reason for the pattern. (c) State why this does not prove that light is the cause.
markscheme: (a) As light intensity decreases, moss cover increases (negative correlation); levels off at about 45% below 200 lux (1)
(b) Moss tolerates shade / is outcompeted by light-demanding plants / dries out in bright light (1)
(c) Other factors change along the transect (e.g. humidity, soil moisture, temperature) (1)
Correlation does not show causation without a controlled experiment (1)
items.tactic: Unfamiliar context: find the syllabus idea being tested, quote the data (with units) when you describe a trend, then explain it with that idea. One marking point per linked step.
